title: An Update on Anti-Cheat
body:
# An Update on Anti-Cheat

Hey Raiders, Aleks here.

Before our major update lands on October 8, I want to speak plainly about something that has frustrated both the community and our team: cheating.

Cheating chips away at the challenge and enjoyment that define ARC Raiders, and it spoils the experience for everyone who plays by the rules. Embark treats this issue with real weight, and we commit significant time and resources to the continuing battle against unfair play.

The cheat market never stands still. People who build and sell cheats make money off players, frequently packaging malware alongside their tools, and each time we strengthen our defenses, they shift tactics to get around them. We keep shifting too. Our anti-cheat team keeps growing and stays focused on spotting and shutting down new cheats, sealing off the routes they exploit, and stacking up obstacles that make cheating more difficult and less rewarding. This is work we intend to keep doing for as long as our games remain live.

We've given you glimpses of this work through occasional updates, but we recognize that simply telling you we're on it falls short. Part of this is deliberate, since revealing too much about our anti-cheat systems can hand cheaters a roadmap for adapting. At other times, we're quietly building and testing things before they go live.

Our quiet doesn't mean we don't care. Today we want to give you a clearer picture of where progress has been made and where our efforts continue to go.

# Detection

Our systems for catching cheats keep getting stronger with each passing month. Alongside kernel-level protection from Denuvo and detection work from Anybrain, we rely on a growing collection of in-house models built on machine learning and other data sources.

These systems work in tandem to flag suspicious behavior and build up confidence before any action is taken, and they let us keep sharpening detection as fresh cheats surface. None of this runs on full autopilot. A human stays in the loop through the appeals process to make sure sanctions get applied fairly.

Looking further ahead, we want to bring in additional anti-cheat tools, including Elytra, which is currently undergoing small-scale testing in THE FINALS. Early signs point to real promise, and we're working toward the point where we can bring this testing to ARC Raiders too.

# Taking action

Once we've gathered enough evidence that a player is cheating, we act. Over recent months, we've sharpened our ability to spot and sanction accounts running cheat software, along with accounts tied to economy exploits. We've also kept working to make it harder for repeat offenders to just spin up a new account and jump back in.

Early on, we were too hesitant to hand out permanent bans to first-time cheaters. We've heard the community's frustration, and we agree that we should have approached this differently. Permanent bans are now the standard response for every known cheat program, and as a matter of policy, any account caught cheating gets permanently banned. No warnings. No second chances.

We've also expanded our use of license restrictions. These stop the specific copy of the game tied to a sanction from being used on another account. We've tightened our handling of linked accounts too. If an account has ever been connected to a banned copy of the game, that account also receives a permanent ban.

# Hardware bans

Hardware bans form another piece of our sanctions toolkit. When we gather enough evidence that a single machine is being used to cheat, we can block the game from running on that system entirely. We keep hardening our detection abilities, and we recently managed to lower the threshold needed before these bans get applied.

We're also actively developing a solution that will let us target more systems with a hardware ban. This should cut down on repeat offenders returning on the same machines. We aim to roll this out later in the year, and it should let us apply sanctions to nearly every system caught running cheat software.

Hardware bans aren't a cure-all, and cheat makers constantly look for ways around our restrictions. Our job, as it always has been, is to push out fixes as fast as possible so hardware bans stay as dependable and effective as they can be.

# Why some bans aren't immediate

We understand the frustration of watching hackers stream or post footage of themselves cheating without seeing an immediate ban.

Anti-cheat systems can't ban a player the instant something looks off. Doing so would risk wrongly banning players who are actually playing fair. The system studies behavior across multiple instances so we can reach a high level of certainty that fair play has been compromised. Once we reach that certainty, we issue a permanent ban.

Our team personally reviews videos and streams that clearly break our rules. We regularly check footage posted on YouTube and other platforms and take action whenever it offers clear proof of cheating. So if you spot a clip of someone cheating online, know that we may already be handling it behind the scenes.

# Tackling other forms of unfair play

Cheating isn't the only way a raid can be spoiled. Queue teaming, where players coordinate to land in the same solo lobby and gang up on Raiders who queued alone, has been another major source of community frustration. We've spent months building up our detection capabilities to the point where we can reliably spot teaming groups.

A few days ago, we began separating known teaming groups during matchmaking. Five days later, we recorded an 85% drop in players engaging in this behavior. Spoiled raids fell from roughly 1 in 50 down to 1 in 300, with no meaningful effect on queue times.

Teaming up with someone you happen to meet mid-raid through proximity chat still counts as fair play. What we're targeting is coordination arranged with another player before the raid even starts, specifically to gain an unfair edge in that session.

We're continuing to look into ways to cut down on matchmaking abuse, and we use what we learn to improve things for Raiders playing fair. We're making strong progress here so far and will keep you posted as things develop.

# An ongoing fight

Cheating in video games is a multi-billion dollar industry, and it will never disappear completely. What we can do is make cheating as hard, as costly, and as short-lived as possible.

We built ARC Raiders with genuine love and care for the craft, and watching it get exploited by cheaters angers us just as much as it angers you. We are making progress, and we'll keep working to spot cheating faster, act on it more quickly, make it harder for repeat offenders to come back, and improve things for Raiders who play fair.

The work goes on, we're seeing real results, and we'll keep you posted as we make further headway.

Thanks for listening,

Aleks

Executive Producer, ARC Raiders
